lessons.bridge_to_teach: Define a transformation, composition, identity and inverse by acting on explicit tuples. Build finite composition tables before the group name. State the carrier and the quantity preserved.

worked_example.task_and_answer: On ordered real pairs let R(x,y)=(y,x). I and R satisfy II=I,IR=RI=R,RR=I. For(2,5), R gives(5,2), preserving sum7 and squared norm29; inverse is R.

guided_practice.task_and_answer: On ordered triples let T(x,y,z)=(z,x,y). T(1,2,3)=(3,1,2), T^2 gives(2,3,1), T^3=I. The three operations compose by exponents modulo3 and preserve sum6 and squared norm14.

diagnostic.task_and_answer: The set{I,T} is not closed since T*T=T^2 is missing. A rule without a carrier or composition law is insufficient for a symmetry claim.

worked_example.task_and_answer: (C_b,C_c)=(2,1) gives(S,A)=(3,1). Transfer(1,-1) yields(3,0),(S,A)=(3,3); S fixed,A increased2, odd class retained. Reverse by(-1,1).

guided_practice.task_and_answer: (-1,3) gives S=2,A=-4; after transfer(0,2),S=2,A=-2. Both represent even class0 mod2. Recover the input as((S+A)/2,(S-A)/2)=(-1,3).

diagnostic.task_and_answer: A parity class alone loses the integer A; retain A or quotient representative plus its even displacement. S=1,A=0 cannot decode integer carries. Carry parity is not detector antipodal parity.

worked_example.task_and_answer: alpha1^2=alpha2^2=2 and alpha1 dot alpha2=-1, so Cartan=[[2,-1],[-1,2]]. All six roots are the signed differences e_i-e_j. q=(2,-3,1)=2alpha1-alpha2.

guided_practice.task_and_answer: q=(-1,3,-2)=-alpha1+2alpha2; reconstruct each component. alpha1+alpha2=(1,0,-1) has norm squared2; alpha1 dot(alpha1+alpha2)=1. Verify zero sum for every root.

diagnostic.task_and_answer: Zero-sum(1/2,-1/2,0) lies in the real plane but not its integer root lattice. Any integer q=(x,y,z) with sum0 equals x alpha1-z alpha2; show this componentwise.

lessons.bridge_to_teach: Define centered weights u_i=e_i-(1,1,1)/3. Explicitly define P2=Z u1+Z u2 with u3=-u1-u2, and Q2 as integer zero-sum vectors. Show a u1+b u2 is integral iff a+b=0 mod3, giving three classes without assuming an abstract quotient theorem.

worked_example.task_and_answer: u1=(2,-1,-1)/3; u1-u2=alpha1. u1 and2u1 are nonintegral but3u1=(2,-1,-1) is a root-lattice vector. Representatives0,u1,2u1 have classes0,1,2; addition is modulo3.

guided_practice.task_and_answer: u1+u2=(1,1,-2)/3 has class2. 2u1+u2=(1,0,-1)=alpha1+alpha2 has class0. u2-u1=(-1,1,0) lies in Q2, so u1 andu2 share a class. Retain coefficients(a,b) when making a quotient view.

diagnostic.task_and_answer: The three displayed weights u1,u2,u3 are three channels in one nonzero quotient class, not the three quotient classes. A root step leaves class unchanged but changes the vector; quotient label alone cannot reconstruct it.

worked_example.task_and_answer: Formal e1,e2 have sum1 and differencealpha1. Centering givesu1,u2. A source-compatible lift of residue(1,0,0) mod3 is(1,0,0)+3(0,1,-1)=(1,3,-3), reducing to the same residue. It is not a new face-area ratio.

guided_practice.task_and_answer: Use lift(1,0,0)+3(-1,0,1)=(-2,0,3); reduction mod3 again(1,0,0), and retained lift digit(-1,0,1) reconstructs it. Separately record an arbitrary family tag F2 and detector parity -1; neither is determined by A mod2 or weight class.

diagnostic.task_and_answer: There are27 compatible lifts when all three digits vary in{-1,0,1}; this does not mean27 primitive channel types. The source three primitive lifts are not the three projective ray coordinates; do not identify them just because both use triples.

worked_example.task_and_answer: U=diag(i,-i), U†=diag(-i,i), U†U=I. On(1+i,2-i), output=(-1+i,-1-2i); norm squared2+5=7 is retained and U† restores the input.

guided_practice.task_and_answer: V=(1/sqrt2)[[1,i],[i,1]], V†=(1/sqrt2)[[1,-i],[-i,1]]. Multiply to get I. V(1,i)=(0,sqrt2*i), norms2; V† restores(1,i). Also V(2,0)=(sqrt2,i sqrt2), norms4.

diagnostic.task_and_answer: Transpose alone gives V^T=V but V^T V=[[0,i],[i,0]], not I. Nonzero phases cannot be dropped during recovery.

worked_example.task_and_answer: For diag(i,-i), determinant1. Color diag(i,-i,1) and weak I2 give determinant product1. Central diag(z^a I3,z^b I2) scales the top form by z^(3a+2b); a=-2,b=3 gives exponent0.

guided_practice.task_and_answer: Color diag(-1,-1,1), weak diag(i,-i) have determinants1 and1, hence preserve the top form. a=2,b=-3 also gives zero exponent. a=1,b=0 with z=i gives determinant i^3=-i, so it fails.

diagnostic.task_and_answer: A determinant-one matrix need not preserve norm: diag(2,1/2) has determinant1 but sends(1,0) to(2,0). Both the Hermitian and top-form conditions are needed; all-phase lock is stronger than one accidental phase test.

worked_example.task_and_answer: Toy k mod3 from addition mod6 lists outputs0,1,2,0,1,2 and kernel{0,3}; it is not the source quotient. For source z=zeta, take g3=zeta^2 I3,g2=-I2. Determinants=zeta^6=1 and(-1)^2=1; both Phi blocks are I.

guided_practice.task_and_answer: Toy k mod2 has kernel{0,2,4}, retaining input label for reconstruction. Source z=zeta^2 gives g3=zeta^4 I3,g2=I2; source z=-1 gives g3=I3,g2=-I2. Verify both determinants/actions, then complete the six-row table k=0..5 using zeta^6=1. Full answer in powers of zeta for k=0..5: z exponents(0,1,2,3,4,5), g3 scalar exponents(0,2,4,0,2,4), g2 scalar exponents(0,3,0,3,0,3). Every determinant and both block actions equal1; retain k because the image alone loses the kernel member.

diagnostic.task_and_answer: C14-KER-D1 is the mod2 toy check. For any source kernel member, identity output forces g3=z^2I3 and g2=z^-3I2; det g3=1 forces z^6=1. Thus these six exhaust this map kernel. This proves the stated finite kernel under its contract, not a unique physical global form.
